Part of a coordinated July 26-28, 2026 campaign against 30+ Minnesota municipal water/wastewater utilities (and facilities in other states); each issue names a different city, so one record per victim city - reviewer may want a shared campaign_id. The issue's pipeline summary says Oct 14-15, 2024, but NPR, Wired, DysruptionHub and the GovInfoSecurity link (2026-07-30) all date the attacks to late July 2026 -> 2026 used, dbir 2027. Attribution: a leaked WaterISAC memo (citing Minnesota Fusion Center and CISA) tied the attacks to Iranian state-sponsored hackers (CyberAv3ngers or Handala, IRGC-linked) -> actor State-affiliated, country IR, no single name; not formally confirmed by the government. Motive not stated -> Unknown. NPR cites experts that internet-exposed devices with default credentials were likely targeted, but this is not confirmed for this victim -> hacking variety/vector Unknown. Assets: PLCs/ICS at water facilities -> N - PLC, asset role OT. No data disclosure reported -> no confidentiality attribute despite the Breach label. NAICS re-coded from 92 to 221310 (water supply) following the analyst comment on issue 23907 ('naics 2213'); victim is the city (government Local) operating the utility. Sources fetched: issue summaries; WebFetch budget ran out before StateScoop/Wired could be re-read directly. Braham: pump station failure, manual intervention restored operations within hours -> availability Interruption (Hours). Integrity Unknown (control logic tampering implied but not described). Discovery: plant failure noticed by operators -> internal Infrastructure monitoring (assumption). Employee count estimated 11 to 100 for a city of 1,700 - not sourced.

summary: On or about July 26-28, 2026, the City of Braham, Minnesota (population about 1,700) was one of more than 30 Minnesota municipal water and wastewater utilities hit by a coordinated cyberattack on remotely accessible, cellular-connected industrial control equipment. Braham's pump station failed, briefly threatening water service until staff restored operations manually within hours; water quality was not affected. A leaked WaterISAC memo tied the campaign to Iranian state-sponsored hackers, and CISA urged utilities to remove internet-exposed PLCs.
